title: BGP Route Reflection: An Alternative to Full Mesh Internal BGP (IBGP)
summary: Describes route reflection, a method that removes the need for a full mesh of internal BGP (IBGP) sessions inside an autonomous system. A full mesh creates a serious scaling problem as the network grows. This document replaces RFC 2796 and RFC 1966. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every person in a big office calling every other person, a few people relay the news. Everyone still hears it, with far fewer calls.

questions: what is a bgp route reflector
how does route reflection avoid loops
subtitle: How a few BGP routers can relay routes inside an AS so that not every router needs a session with every other.

tldr.problem: Internal BGP normally needs a full mesh of sessions between all BGP speakers in an AS, which needs n*(n-1)/2 IBGP sessions and does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A route reflector is allowed to re-advertise IBGP-learned routes to other IBGP peers. Its peers are split into clients and non-clients, and two new optional non-transitive attributes, ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST, prevent loops.
tldr.outcome: Clients only need a session with their reflector. RFC 4456 obsoletes RFC 1966 and RFC 2796, and has since been updated by RFC 7606.

today: RFC 4456 is listed as a Draft Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2796 and RFC 1966 and has been updated by RFC 7606.

sections.title: The Full-Mesh Problem
sections.content:
Normally all BGP speakers inside one autonomous system must be fully meshed, and any external routing information must be passed on to every other router in that AS. For n speakers that means n*(n-1)/2 unique IBGP sessions. The RFC says this does not scale when many speakers exchange a large volume of routing information.

Route reflection is offered as another alternative to the full mesh. It lets a BGP speaker, the route reflector, advertise IBGP-learned routes to certain IBGP peers. That changes the commonly understood concept of IBGP and adds two new optional non-transitive BGP attributes to prevent loops.
sections.plainLanguage: If every kid in a big class had to phone every other kid, the phones would never stop ringing. Route reflection picks a few kids to pass messages along instead.

sections.title: Design Criteria
sections.content:
Route reflection was designed to meet three criteria, motivated by operational experience of a very large, topology-rich network with many external connections.

  • Simplicity: it must be simple to configure and easy to understand.
  • Easy transition: it must be possible to move from a full mesh without changing topology or AS. The RFC calls this an unfortunate management overhead of the confederation technique in its reference [3].
  • Compatibility: peers that do not support it must be able to stay in the AS without losing any BGP routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: The new idea had to be easy to set up, easy to switch to, and friendly to old equipment that did not know about it.

sections.title: Reflectors, Clients and Clusters
sections.content:
The basic idea is simple. In an AS with three IBGP speakers (RTR-A, RTR-B and RTR-C), IBGP speakers normally do not re-advertise IBGP-learned routes to other IBGP speakers. If RTR-C is allowed to do so, it can reflect the routes learned from RTR-A to RTR-B and the other way round, so the IBGP session between RTR-A and RTR-B is no longer needed.

A speaker that does this is a route reflector (RR) and the route is a reflected route. The internal peers of an RR fall into two groups: client peers and non-client peers. An RR together with its clients forms a cluster. The non-client peers must be fully meshed, but the clients need not be.
sections.plainLanguage: The reflector is the class messenger. Its clients just tell the messenger, and the messenger tells everyone else.

sections.title: How Reflection Works
sections.content:
When an RR receives a route from an IBGP peer, it first selects the best path using its normal path selection rule. What it does next depends on who sent the best path.

  • From a non-client peer: reflect it to all the clients.
  • From a client peer: reflect it to all the non-client peers and also to the other clients. That is why clients do not need to be fully meshed.

An AS can have many RRs, and an RR treats other RRs like any other internal BGP speaker. In a simple setup the backbone is split into clusters, the RRs are fully meshed as non-client peers of each other, and each client keeps an IBGP session only with the RR in its cluster.

Conventional BGP speakers that do not understand route reflection can be clients or non-clients, which allows a gradual migration. You can start with one designated RR and configure the others as ordinary IBGP peers, then add clusters over time.

A cluster usually has a single RR and is identified by that RR's BGP Identifier. Because that is a single point of failure, several RRs in one cluster can be given the same 4-byte CLUSTER_ID so that an RR can discard routes from other RRs in its cluster.
sections.plainLanguage: The messenger repeats what it hears to the right groups. Old-style kids who do not know the game can still join in, and a cluster can have a backup messenger.

sections.title: Avoiding Routing Information Loops
sections.content:
Through misconfiguration, reflected routes could form redistribution loops. Two new optional, non-transitive attributes detect them.

ORIGINATOR_ID (type code 9) is 4 bytes long and is created by an RR when it reflects a route. It carries the BGP Identifier of the route's originator in the local AS. A speaker SHOULD NOT create one if it already exists, and a router that recognizes it SHOULD ignore a route that arrives with its own BGP Identifier as the ORIGINATOR_ID.

CLUSTER_LIST (type code 10) is a sequence of CLUSTER_ID values showing the reflection path the route has passed. An RR MUST prepend its local CLUSTER_ID when it reflects a route, creating the list if it is empty. If the local CLUSTER_ID is already in the list, the advertisement SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets stamped with who started it and which groups it has passed through. If a messenger sees its own stamp, it knows the message has gone in a circle and drops it.

sections.title: Impact on Route Selection
sections.content:
The BGP tie-breaking rules from RFC 4271 are modified in two ways. If a route carries ORIGINATOR_ID, then in step f) it SHOULD be treated as the BGP Identifier of the speaker that advertised the route. A new rule SHOULD be inserted between steps f) and g): prefer the route with the shorter CLUSTER_LIST. A route without the attribute counts as length zero.

When reflecting, an RR SHOULD NOT modify NEXT_HOP, AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF or MED, and the loop-prevention attributes must not be modifiable by configuration, because changes could cause routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: When two routes look equally good, the one that went through fewer messengers wins. Messengers must pass notes along without changing them.

sections.title: Configuration and Deployment
sections.content:
BGP has no way for a client to identify itself dynamically as a client of an RR, so the simplest approach is manual configuration. The RR summarizes routing information by reflecting only its best path, which is a key part of how it addresses scaling.

Because MEDs are not always comparable and IGP metrics can differ for each router, some reflection topologies may not choose the same routes as a full IBGP mesh would. The RFC suggests keeping intra-cluster IGP metrics better than inter-cluster ones and keeping a full mesh within the cluster, and handling MEDs by setting local preference to reflect them, making AS-path lengths differ, or using community-based policies. It also notes that one could argue this is overly restrictive, as long as there are no routing loops.

The reflection topology should be congruent with the network topology when multiple paths exist for a prefix. A commonly used approach is reflection by Point of Presence (POP): each POP has its own route reflectors serving its clients, and all the reflectors are fully meshed.
sections.plainLanguage: You have to tell each kid who their messenger is. Put the messengers where the real roads are, so messages take sensible routes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that this extension to BGP does not change the underlying security issues inherent in existing IBGP. It points to RFC 4271 and RFC 2385 for those issues and adds no new security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing messages through a messenger does not make the messages any safer or less safe than before.

items.label: ORIGINATOR_ID
items.desc: 4 bytes; BGP Identifier of the route's originator in the local AS. Optional, non-transitive.

items.label: CLUSTER_LIST
items.desc: Sequence of CLUSTER_IDs the route has passed through; each RR prepends its own. Optional, non-transitive.
